extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and informed general readers evaluating or presenting a proposed solution to the quadrature of the circle
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and expectations for producing or judging a claimed proof/solution of the quadrature of the circle (i.e., an exact relation between diameter and circumference). Emphasises experimental testability, commensurable geometric constructions, numerical consistency, and rejection of authority in favour of demonstrable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental testability (measurement verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments and claims should be testable by experiment or measurement (e.g., using a wire thread to determine circumference and diameter; stakes and measuring tape as practical tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly appeals to simple experiments (wrapping a thread around the disc, measuring diameters, comparing rectangles built from those lengths) as a way to convince oneself of the truth or fallacy of a proposed relation. He also warns that naive experiments can be fallacious unless properly interpreted; experiments should support, not contradict, the claimed exact result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact commensurability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid solution must show an exact (commensurable) ratio between diameter and circumference rather than an incommensurable/approximate decimal expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects the orthodox view that the relation is incommensurable and demands a precise commensurable relation (he proposes 3 1/8 for circumference when diameter = 1). He frames the goal as demonstrating 'exactly the relation'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of commensurable geometric constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstration should connect the circle to other geometrical figures via commensurable constructions (e.g., inscribed regular hexagon, right-angled triangles with side ratios 3:4, squares on triangle sides) to create a chain of commensurable figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text constructs explicit diagrams (inscribed hexagon, right triangles with sides in ratio 3:4, squares on sides) and uses these to relate areas and perimeters; a proper demonstration should produce such explicit geometric constructions that exhibit exact relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inscribed regular polygons as a fixed invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the perimeter of certain inscribed regular polygons (notably the regular hexagon) as a fixed, known quantity to relate to the circumference, and employ that relation in argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly uses the perimeter of an inscribed hexagon (perimeter = 3 when diameter = 1) to derive consequences for the circumference under different hypotheses and to argue that only a specific value yields exact agreement (he contrasts approximations with his chosen commensurable value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric consistency across derived quantities (area, circumference, diameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct solution must produce internal numeric consistency between circumference, area, diameter, and related derived quantities in selected unit choices (e.g., when diameter = 4, circumference and area should agree numerically under the claimed relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author demonstrates checks such as: if diameter = 4 then under his hypothesis circumference = area numerically; he uses multiplicative checks (half circumference times half diameter, or square of diameter times assumed area-per-unit) to show consistency. A valid proof should similarly show such consistent cross-checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on authority; appeal to evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept or reject claims on the basis of authority; the matter must be settled by clear evidence and demonstrable reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay explicitly rejects 'the highest authorities' as decisive, arguing that evidence and reproducible demonstrations are the appropriate standard. The author invites readers (masters and disciples alike) to examine the evidence themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mere approximation — require exact demonstration rather than limits/approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: An acceptable proof must not rest on approximations that only approach the claimed relation; it must demonstrate exact equality rather than arbitrarily close approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises hypotheses that yield arbitrarily close approximations to the arc or circumference but never exact equality, and insists that one must identify the single arithmetical symbols (he asserts 3.125) that 'must represent the true circumference' rather than settle for infinite decimal approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit algebraic/numeric computation and formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstration should include explicit algebraic computations (numerical substitutions, multiplications, areas, perimeters) to make the argument concrete and checkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the excerpt the author works through numerical examples (e.g., 3.1416 vs 3.125, area values 0.7854 vs 0.78125, multiplications with chosen diameters) — a valid proof should supply analogous explicit calculations so readers can verify each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply clear diagrams and step-by-step geometric constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include labelled diagrams and stepwise geometric constructions (centres, radii, inscribed polygons, triangles, squares) that are referenced in the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text refers to diagrams (Fig. XXVI, XXVII), describes constructions (circle with centre O, diameter AB, right triangles with specific side ratios) and draws conclusions from those constructions. The rubric expects such visual, constructive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and reproducibility by competent arithmeticians/geometricians
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument should be framed so that any competent arithmetician or geometrician can follow, reproduce, and judge the result independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author maintains that 'any man who is a fair arithmetician and geometrician, may be made as competent to judge of the truth' and thus the proof should not depend on obscure methods but be reproducible by straightforward calculation and construction.
